output:
Here's a draft you can post as is or tweak:

---

**Title: The part nobody teaches you**

I've read this thread for a long time and never posted, but this month there's one that won't leave me alone.

I'm a community pharmacist in a small independent pharmacy, just me and one tech. Mrs. H was one of my blister pack patients. She was in her eighties and had been coming to us for seven years. Every Thursday, same routine. She lived alone, walked with a cane with tennis balls on the feet, and took eleven medications, so her packs were never small.

And every Thursday she brought me something. Usually homemade cake. Once it was a jar of pickles, and I honestly had no idea what to do with them, but I took them like it was a gift from a king. One Ramadan she remembered without me ever mentioning it. She handed me a cake wrapped in foil with my name on it and told me not to touch it until sunset. I still think about that.

A couple of years ago a new doctor added a medication that interacted with her warfarin. I caught it, called him, and it got changed. That's the job. It's what we're trained for and I didn't think much of it. But she told everybody that I saved her life. I kept saying I just did my job and she would wave her hand at me like I was being silly.

She passed away at the end of last month. This week her daughter came in to return the unused packs and the glucometer. We do this all the time, it's routine. I was doing the paperwork the normal way, thinking about the normal things, how to document it, how to dispose of it properly.

Then she handed me a card. Inside, in her mother's handwriting from a long time ago, it said "for my Arabic daughter." She had written it and never gave it to me.

I went to the back room and cried. My tech covered the counter for ten minutes and never said a word about it afterwards. I appreciated that more than she knows.

In school they teach us pharmacology, interactions, counselling, how to read a prescription that a doctor wrote in a hurry. Nobody teaches you how to say goodbye to a patient. And we're told, maybe not directly but you learn it, that we shouldn't get too attached. But when you see someone every single week for seven years, what are you supposed to do? You know her kids, her bad knee, what she's worried about, what she does when she's lonely. You know her better than a lot of people in her life do.

My father is a pharmacist in Egypt, and he knew every family in his neighbourhood. They called him at home, they brought him food, they invited him to weddings and funerals. When I moved to Canada I think I assumed it would be more professional and distant here. It's not. Not in a small pharmacy anyway. Maybe it can't be.

I'm still not sure what to do with all this. I came home and I couldn't stop thinking about her walking in with the cane and the foil package. I'm not sad exactly. It's more that I'm grateful, and it's a strange feeling to carry around.

So I wanted to ask here. Has anyone had a patient like this? How did you handle it when they passed? Do you go to the funeral, or send a card, or just carry it quietly? And does it get easier, or do you just get better at going to the back room?

Thanks for reading.

---

I left out her name, age, ethnicity, the daughter's name, your tech's name, your city, and the exact dates, so nothing points to her. If you'd like it shorter, the paragraph about your father is the easiest to trim, though I think it's one of the strongest parts.
